entries.content_plain: 5. seek not Beth-el-- that is, the calves at Beth-el. Gilgal-- (See on Am 4:4 ). Beer-sheba-- in Judah on the southern frontier towards Edom. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12573"/><div sID="gen23168" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12573"/><hi type="bold">9. strengtheneth the spoiled--</hi>literally, "spoil" or "devastation": hence the "person spoiled." Winer, Maurer, and the best modern critics translate, "maketh devastation (or destruction) suddenly to arise," literally, "maketh it to gleam forth like the dawn." Ancient versions support English Version. The Hebrew is elsewhere used, to make, to shine, to make glad: and as English Version here (<reference osisRef="Ps.39.13">Psa 39:13</reference>), "recover strength."<div eID="gen23168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23169" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the spoiled shall come--</hi>"devastation," or "destruction shall come upon" [Maurer]. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12577"/><div sID="gen23177" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12577"/><hi type="bold">13. the prudent--</hi>the spiritually wise.<div eID="gen23177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23178" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall keep silence--</hi>not mere silence of tongue, but the prudent shall keep himself quiet from taking part in any public or private affairs which he can avoid: as it is "an evil time," and one in which all law is set at naught. <reference osisRef="Eph.5.16">Ep 5:16</reference> refers to this. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12583"/><div sID="gen23195" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12583"/><hi type="bold">19. As if a man did flee ... a lion, and a bear met him--</hi>Trying to escape one calamity, he falls into another. This perhaps implies that in <reference osisRef="Amos.5.18">Am 5:18</reference> their ironical desire for the day of the Lord was as if it would be an escape from existing calamities. The coming of the day of the Lord would be good news to us, if true: for we have served God (that is, the golden calves). So do hypocrites flatter themselves as to death and judgment, as if these would be a relief from existing ills of life. The lion may from generosity spare the prostrate, but the bear spares none (compare <reference osisRef="Job.20.24">Job 20:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.24.18">Is 24:18</reference>).<div eID="gen23195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23196" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">leaned ... on the wall--</hi>on the side wall of the house, to support himself from falling. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12588"/><div sID="gen23208" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12588"/><hi type="bold">25-26. Have ye offered? &c.--</hi>Yes: ye have. "But (all the time with strange inconsistency) ye have borne (aloft in solemn pomp) the tabernacle (that is, the portable shrine, or model tabernacle: small enough not to be detected by Moses; compare <reference osisRef="Acts.19.24">Ac 19:24</reference>) of your Molech" (that idol is "your" god; I am not, though ye go through the form of presenting offerings to Me). The question, "Have ye," is not a denial (for they did offer in the wilderness to Jehovah sacrifices of the cattle which they took with them in their nomad life there, <reference osisRef="Exod.24.4">Ex 24:4</reference>; Nu 7:1-89; 9:1, &c.), but a strong affirmation (compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.27">1Sa 2:27</reference>, 28; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.20">Jr 31:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.4">Eze 20:4</reference>). The sin of Israel in Amos' time is the very sin of their forefathers, mocking God with worship, while at the same time worshipping idols (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.39">Eze 20:39</reference>). It was clandestine in Moses' time, else he would have put it down; he was aware generally of their unfaithfulness, though not knowing the particulars (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.21">De 31:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.27">27</reference>).<div eID="gen23208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23209" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Molech ... Chiun--</hi>"Molech" means "king" answering to Mars [Bengel]; the Sun [Jablonski]; Saturn, the same as "Chiun" [Maurer]. The Septuagint translates "Chiun" into Remphan, as Stephen quotes it (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.42">Ac 7:42</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.7.43">43</reference>). The same god often had different names. Molech is the Ammonite name; Chiun, the Arabic and Persian name, written also Chevan. In an Arabic lexicon Chiun means "austere"; so astrologers represented Saturn as a planet baleful in his influence. Hence the Phoenicians offered human sacrifices to him, children especially; so idolatrous Israel also. Rimmon was the Syrian name (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.18">2Ki 5:18</reference>); pronounced as Remvan, or "Remphan," just as Chiun was also Chevan. Molech had the form of a king; Chevan, or Chiun, of a star [Grotius]. Remphan was the Egyptian name for Saturn: hence the Septuagint translator of Amos gave the Egyptian name for the Hebrew, being an Egyptian. [Hodius II, De Bibliorum Textibus Originalibus. 4.115]. The same as the Nile, of which the Egyptians made the star Saturn the representative [Harenberg]. Bengel considers Remphan or Rephan akin to Teraphim and Remphis, the name of a king of Egypt. The Hebrews became infected with Sabeanism, the oldest form of idolatry, the worship of the Saba or starry hosts, in their stay in the Arabian desert, where Job notices its prevalence (<reference osisRef="Job.31.26">Job 31:26</reference>); in opposition, in <reference osisRef="Amos.5.27">Am 5:27</reference>, Jehovah declares Himself "the God of hosts."<div eID="gen23209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23210" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the star of your god--</hi>R. Isaac Caro says all the astrologers represented Saturn as the star of Israel. Probably there was a figure of a star on the head of the image of the idol, to represent the planet Saturn; hence "images" correspond to "star" in the parallel clause. A star in hieroglyphics represents God (<reference osisRef="Num.24.17">Nu 24:17</reference>). "Images" are either a Hebraism for "image," or refer to the many images made to represent Chiun. <div eID="gen23210" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 25-26. Have ye offered? &c.-- Yes: ye have. "But (all the time with strange inconsistency) ye have borne (aloft in solemn pomp) the tabernacle (that is, the portable shrine, or model tabernacle: small enough not to be detected by Moses; compare Ac 19:24 ) of your Molech" (that idol is "your" god; I am not, though ye go through the form of presenting offerings to Me). The question, "Have ye," is not a denial (for they did offer in the wilderness to Jehovah sacrifices of the cattle which they took with them in their nomad life there, Ex 24:4 ; Nu 7:1-89; 9:1, &c.), but a strong affirmation (compare 1Sa 2:27 , 28; Jr 31:20 ; Eze 20:4 ). The sin of Israel in Amos' time is the very sin of their forefathers, mocking God with worship, while at the same time worshipping idols (compare Eze 20:39 ). It was clandestine in Moses' time, else he would have put it down; he was aware generally of their unfaithfulness, though not knowing the particulars ( De 31:21 , 27 ). Molech ... Chiun-- "Molech" means "king" answering to Mars [Bengel]; the Sun [Jablonski]; Saturn, the same as "Chiun" [Maurer]. The Septuagint translates "Chiun" into Remphan, as Stephen quotes it ( Ac 7:42 , 43 ). The same god often had different names. Molech is the Ammonite name; Chiun, the Arabic and Persian name, written also Chevan. In an Arabic lexicon Chiun means "austere"; so astrologers represented Saturn as a planet baleful in his influence. Hence the Phoenicians offered human sacrifices to him, children especially; so idolatrous Israel also. Rimmon was the Syrian name ( 2Ki 5:18 ); pronounced as Remvan, or "Remphan," just as Chiun was also Chevan. Molech had the form of a king; Chevan, or Chiun, of a star [Grotius]. Remphan was the Egyptian name for Saturn: hence the Septuagint translator of Amos gave the Egyptian name for the Hebrew, being an Egyptian. [Hodius II, De Bibliorum Textibus Originalibus. 4.115]. The same as the Nile, of which the Egyptians made the star Saturn the representative [Harenberg]. Bengel considers Remphan or Rephan akin to Teraphim and Remphis, the name of a king of Egypt. The Hebrews became infected with Sabeanism, the oldest form of idolatry, the worship of the Saba or starry hosts, in their stay in the Arabian desert, where Job notices its prevalence ( Job 31:26 ); in opposition, in Am 5:27 , Jehovah declares Himself "the God of hosts." the star of your god-- R. Isaac Caro says all the astrologers represented Saturn as the star of Israel. Probably there was a figure of a star on the head of the image of the idol, to represent the planet Saturn; hence "images" correspond to "star" in the parallel clause. A star in hieroglyphics represents God ( Nu 24:17 ). "Images" are either a Hebraism for "image," or refer to the many images made to represent Chiun.
entries.reader_content_plain: 25-26. Have ye offered? &c.-- Yes: ye have. "But (all the time with strange inconsistency) ye have borne (aloft in solemn pomp) the tabernacle (that is, the portable shrine, or model tabernacle: small enough not to be detected by Moses; compare Ac 19:24 ) of your Molech" (that idol is "your" god; I am not, though ye go through the form of presenting offerings to Me). The question, "Have ye," is not a denial (for they did offer in the wilderness to Jehovah sacrifices of the cattle which they took with them in their nomad life there, Ex 24:4 ; Nu 7:1-89; 9:1, &c.), but a strong affirmation (compare 1Sa 2:27 , 28; Jr 31:20 ; Eze 20:4 ). The sin of Israel in Amos' time is the very sin of their forefathers, mocking God with worship, while at the same time worshipping idols (compare Eze 20:39 ). It was clandestine in Moses' time, else he would have put it down; he was aware generally of their unfaithfulness, though not knowing the particulars ( De 31:21 , 27 ). Molech ... Chiun-- "Molech" means "king" answering to Mars [Bengel]; the Sun [Jablonski]; Saturn, the same as "Chiun" [Maurer]. The Septuagint translates "Chiun" into Remphan, as Stephen quotes it ( Ac 7:42 , 43 ). The same god often had different names. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12589"/><div sID="gen23211" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12589"/><hi type="bold">27. beyond Damascus--</hi>In <reference osisRef="Acts.7.43">Ac 7:43</reference> it is "beyond Babylon," which includes beyond Damascus. In Amos' time, Damascus was the object of Israel's fear because of the Syrian wars. Babylon was not yet named as the place of their captivity. Stephen supplies this name. Their place of exile was in fact, as he states, "beyond Babylon," in Halah and Habor by the river Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.6">2Ki 17:6</reference>; compare here <reference osisRef="Amos.1.5">Am 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.3">4:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.14">6:14</reference>). The road to Assyria lay through "Damascus." It is therefore specified, that not merely shall they be carried captives to Damascus, as they had been by Syrian kings (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.10.32">2Ki 10:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.10.33">33</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.13.7">13:7</reference>), but, beyond that, to a region whence a return was not so possible as from Damascus. They were led captive by Satan into idolatry, therefore God caused them to go captive among idolaters. Compare <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.29">2Ki 15:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.9">16:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.8.4">Is 8:4</reference>, whence it appears Tiglath-pileser attacked Israel and Damascus at the same time at Ahaz' request (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.11">Am 3:11</reference>). <chapter eID="Amos.5"/>
